lines: That's a new step on the path. Lighter than the post, and you don't scuff. You'll have come up from the station end.
I've put my spectacles down in the garden and now I can't see to find them. They'll be by the beans. The gate's round the side.
By the beans still, I should think. I'd go myself, but I'd only tread on them, and then I'd hear the crunch.
Ah. Now I can see you. You're younger than your feet.
Have an apple. Have two, and the water. I sit out here and watch the road, and nobody comes along it to give them to.
There's a lot of folk go by on that road, by the sound. Boots, mostly. A cart, once, with a wheel that wants grease.
I've had the spectacles on all week, and I've not seen one of them yet. I go in at nine. I don't know who started that.
You've not seen a bill-hook? Hooked blade, ash handle. Beech. The old one was ash.
I put it down in the clearing and turned round, and it wasn't there. Fourteen years I've had it. Fifteen, come Michaelmas.
Round the clearing. I've been round twice. Three times, if you count the once I didn't look properly.
That's it. Where was it, in the end?
Stuck in by the point? I don't do that. Not often. Take some wood; I cut more than I burn. More every year, lately. Every month.
I stop at four. Half four, in summer. The light goes wrong under the trees after that, low, from the side, like off a lamp somebody's carrying.
I've locked myself out. I tried the handle twice to be sure, and once more after that, and it's locked.
The spare's under a stone in the garden. I can't think which stone. I've stood here since the milk came. I don't like to turn my back on the house.
Under a stone. One of the four; I've counted, and it's four. They rock if you lean on them, so put each one back the way it was.
Oh, that's it. Let me try it. Yes. It turns. I'll try it again.
Take these. They were my mother's pansies, and they come up whatever I do to them. There. Open. I've tried it twice.
I lock it at nine and I try it at ten. Once I found it open at ten. I'd tried it at nine.
I try it at eleven now as well. It's been locked every time at eleven. I try it at twelve to make sure of eleven.
The hens have laid. First time in a week.
Would you fetch them in from the hen house? There's more about at night than there was, and I'd like them in the bowl before anything else has them.
The hen house, by the farmhouse. The brown one sits on them. Lift her; don't push, she pecks.
Three. That's all of them, then.
Have a couple of apples. I'd give you an egg, but I'd like to see the three of them in the one bowl for a day or two first.
He has his dinner at twelve. He takes his cap off the hook, he goes across to the barn, he counts the sacks, and then it's his tea at five.
It's gone five. I won't knock; he doesn't like it. Would you? Say it's only about his tea.
The big doors. Knock twice, and say it's only about his tea. He'll answer to that, if he's at the end of a row.
Counting. He'll be counting the sacks.
Up at six, kettle on, the hens, his breakfast, the barn, his dinner, the barn. Every day since March. There were twelve in March. Take the water, for that.
He says eleven. There should be twelve, and he won't come in till there's twelve.
The other's in the sheep pen. He carried it there himself on Sunday. Would you fetch it? If I tell him, he'll only start again from one.
In the pen, with the sheep. Don't say I told you. Bring it here, and I'll put it back while he's at his tea.
That's twelve. He'll be out now.
Take this, from the pantry. My mother put it up; I don't know what it is. It's good, whatever it is. She always knew. And two apples.
He came in for his tea. Cap on the hook, washed his hands, ate it all. He sat where he could see the barn door, and I didn't ask.
I knock twice and say it's only about his tea.
Inside, a man's voice says he's counting, and he'll be out when he's finished, and would I please not knock again. He's lost his place. He starts over.
"Eleven," says the voice behind the door. A long wait. A sack dragged across boards. "Eleven."
The big doors are shut. Inside, somebody's moving sacks about, slowly, one at a time, stopping after each.
That's the well, on the green. You'll have seen it? Would you draw me a bucket? My arms aren't what they were.
And taste it. Was it March it started? It was March. It's tasted of something since, and I'd like somebody young to tell me I'm imagining it.
The well, on the green. Is the bucket up? It always is. Let it right down to the bottom; the top of it's no good.
Pennies. It tasted of pennies, didn't it?
That's it. That's exactly it. Take a couple of bottles. It's still good water, whatever it tastes of. We drink it, don't we.
Is it the same next door? I'd know, if I asked. I've not asked. We don't, much, on the green, since March.
Would you knock? It's the next house along. Don't say it was me wanted to know.
The next house along. You've not knocked yet, have you? No. Knock, and ask about the water. Don't say it was me.
Since March. They said March, did they?
And not a word to me in all that time. Take these, and thank you. I'll go round myself tomorrow. I will, won't I.
I've been round. We sat in his kitchen with a pot of tea, pennies and all. Did we talk about it? We did not. We talked about his hens.
I let the bucket right down and wind it up. The water's clear, and cold enough to make my teeth ache.
It smells of pennies. I taste it to be sure. It tastes of them too, like a coin held in the mouth, the way I used to when I was small.
A stone well with a wooden lid. The bucket's up, and the chain's wet all the way to the top.
I knock. A man answers without opening the door.
"Pennies? Since March. We drink it anyway. And would you not knock after the bell, please. We don't answer after the bell. Nobody on the green does."
Nobody comes. The curtains are drawn, and have been for a long time; the sun's faded them in stripes, down the folds.
I'm sorry, this will sound silly. Somebody knocks at my door after the bell. Most nights now. Three knocks, and when I look there's nobody.
I won't go out after. But the plot's soft; there'd be prints. Would you look in the rows, by daylight? You needn't. I'm sorry.
The vegetable plot, past the green. Look in the rows. Sorry, you'll know what a plot looks like.
A glove? And no prints?
That ground takes a cat's prints. Sorry, I'm not saying you didn't look. Have a couple of apples. I'm sorry they're small.
I know that glove. I'm sorry. I'd rather not say whose.
Would you take it next door and ask? Knock three times. No. Sorry. Knock twice.
The next house along. Twice. I'm sorry, I said three before, didn't I. Twice.
His father's. Yes. I'm sorry. I knew, I think, when you held it up.
I'll leave a light in the window tonight. You have this one. It's a good light, and I've others.
Nobody knocked last night. I sat up for it in the chair by the door till the window went grey. I'm sorry. I'm not sure that's better.
I knock twice. The door opens the width of its chain, and a man takes the glove and turns it over for a long time.
"That's my father's," he says. "He went out one night in November to see who was knocking." The door shuts with the glove inside.
The chain's on. Through the gap I can see a coat on a hook and a pair of boots under it, polished, with the laces done up.
There's men sit round a fire out at {place:pryor_camp}, off the road. Nobody lights it. They've sat there since the winter.
I know them. Harry Dade's the big one; he takes three sugars. Ned Ashby does the talking.
Would you put them down? Gently, if there's a way. I don't want to know how.
{place:pryor_camp}. Off the road. You'll see the fire, and you'll see it isn't lit. Ned sits nearest the road. He likes to be first home.
It's done, then.
Don't tell me. Take these. I was keeping them for myself, and I won't be going anywhere I'd need them now.
Harry's mother lays his place at teatime. She lays Ned's as well; he's always round there, that one. I don't go past the house at teatime.
This is a respectable house. Doors shut at nine, no credit, and nobody's things left lying about. There's been a bag in the yard since Sunday.
A traveller's. Nobody's come for it. Would you bring it in? I'd sooner not open it myself. A guest's bag is the guest's business.
In the yard, past the trough. Canvas, with a strap. Bags come in by the front door, as a rule. That one didn't.
Anything with a name in it?
A ticket for Sunday's train, not punched. So he was here for it, and didn't go. Have something from the kitchen. Nobody runs an errand here for nothing.
He had the back room. Left his key on the barrels round the side every morning, like I wouldn't know where to look. Keys hang on the board. That's the rule.
Would you fetch it? I'll let the room. I can't keep a room for a man who sleeps in my yard.
The barrels, round the side. The one nearest the wall. Every morning, same barrel, regular as rent.
Four?
We've three rooms. We've always had three; it's on the board by the door, ONE, TWO, THREE. I'll hang it with the others. I won't be letting it. Take these.
Doors at nine. Some nights there's a knock at the back, after. We don't answer after nine in this house. I leave the key to four on the board, in case.
On top of the barrel nearest the wall: a room key on a wooden tag. The tag says 4. The wood's gone dark where a thumb has held it.
An ale barrel, empty by the sound when I knock on it. The rim's worn bright in one place, where something small has been set down every day.
I'm three short in the pen. I count them morning and evening, and it's been three short since Monday. I've counted it four times, both ways round.
There's a lot camped at {place:hurst_camp}, off the road. Would you go and look? Look, that's all. I'd like to know for certain first.
{place:hurst_camp}. Keep your distance. Look for fleece; they won't have had the sense to burn it.
That's my mark on it. Blue, on the shoulder. That's one of the three, then.
Have two apples. I'll be a minute; I'm counting something.
I'd like them moved on. I can't do it, and there's nobody to send for. I've seen the constable out this way once in two years.
I'm sorry to ask it. I was at school with two of them. Two out of the three.
{place:hurst_camp}, off the road. There's three of them. Be careful. Three's a lot, for one.
It's quiet out that way?
Then take these. The wife was keeping them for the winter; she counted them into the cupboard herself. She'd want you to have them.
I count them at eight now, and again before the bell. Three short, both times. I keep counting in case it comes back the other way.
I've lost my ring out of the dish on the sill. Two pound ten, it was, and Farrant paid it off at a shilling a week.
There was a crow at the window all morning, looking in. They keep what they take at {place:farrant_camp}, off the road.
Would you get it back? They don't like being looked at. I'll see you right for it.
{place:farrant_camp}. They keep it all in a box. Don't ask me how a crow comes by a box. Somebody paid good money for that box once.
That's it. That's mine. Two pound ten.
Teaspoons? Those aren't mine. I wouldn't have them now if they were, at any price. Have these for your trouble. They cost me nothing, so don't thank me.
I keep the window shut now, and the ring on. The crow still comes at ten and looks in. I've taken to drawing the curtain, and curtains wear.
The post's being left in the yard now, not at the door. In the yard. There's a letter out there; I can see the white of it from the window.
Would you bring it in? I don't go out to the yard. It's a long way to the yard, these days.
In the yard. It'll be from my son. He writes on a Thursday. Thursdays, he writes.
From my son. Let's see. The weather's fine, he says. Fine weather, where he is.
And he'll be home on Sunday. Sunday, he says. He says that every week. Have two apples.
I've written back. Would you take it to my sister at {place:vosper_sister}, down the road? She keeps them. She keeps every one.
She won't open the door. Put it through the flap. She knows my hand.
{place:vosper_sister}, down the road. Through the flap. She won't open the door, she won't, so don't stand and wait.
She took it? She took it. Good.
She keeps them in a tin, his and mine, all together. Take the water. Two bottles, there.
Would you ask my sister for the tin? All of them. His and mine.
It's time they were read in the right order. I've been reading them in the wrong one. The wrong one, all this while.
{place:vosper_sister}. She'll put it out on the step for you. That's what she does. She puts it out on the step.
Put it on the table. On the table, there, by his chair.
Take this. It was his, from the dresser. He'd want it used. And an apple.
I've read them all now, in order. I know when he stopped writing. I'm still waiting for Sunday.
He says Sunday in every one. He says it in the last one too.
I put the letter through the flap. It lands on a mat that sounds thick with others.
From inside, a woman's voice: "Thank you. I'll put it with the rest." Her feet don't come any nearer the door.
"She wants the tin," says the voice. "Well. It's hers as much as mine."
The door opens a hand's width, and a biscuit tin heavy with paper is set out on the step. The lid's warm where it's been held.
Nobody comes. Inside, somebody's sitting very still, the way I used to sit when a knock came and I wanted it to go away.
I grew up at {place:hackett_house}. Off the road, that way. It's walls now. That's that.
Would you look inside for me and say what's left? I've not been since, and I'm not going. There. Settled.
{place:hackett_house}. Mind the rubble inside. That's all I'll say about it.
Marks on the door frame. We did that, every birthday. Mother stood us up against it with a book on our heads.
The last one's higher than the rest? There's nobody left to be that tall. Take this. We'll leave it there.
My mother kept a tin under the front step. The rent book, our certificates, a lock of somebody's hair. Everything that mattered went in it.
Would you fetch it? I know what's in it. I'd still like it. Right. Enough about that.
Under the front step at {place:hackett_house}. It was always loose; lean on it and it goes. That's all there is to it.
That's the tin. Rusted shut, is it. It would be.
There. That's the house, with its roof on. Take this; she wouldn't mind. And that's the end of it.
I cut on this side of the road now. I can't see it from here. Done with.
Pencil marks on what's left of the door frame, a name and a height beside each. HACKETT, over and over, in careful capitals.
The highest mark is the newest. The pencil's hardly faded. I'm standing straight against the frame before I think, and I step off.
I've left my scissors in the garden. I was cutting flowers for the table.
Somebody on the road said my name. The short way, the way my husband says it. I came straight in. There was nobody on the road.
Would you fetch them? By the rows. And I won't ask yours. Don't tell me it.
In the garden, by the rows, where I dropped them. If anybody calls you from the road, you don't know them.
Thank you.
In a row? I didn't leave them in a row; I dropped them. Well. Have these, from the same bed. And an apple.
If you hear your name on the road, don't answer it. Don't turn round to it either. That's all I'm saying.
These are for the woodcutter at {place:venn_wood}. Windfalls. He cuts my wood and he won't take a penny for it. Cold for the time of year, isn't it.
Would you leave them on his woodpile? He won't stop to be thanked. He never stops. The evenings are drawing in.
{place:venn_wood}. On top of the woodpile, where he'll see. There's a nip in the air in the mornings now.
Kindling? Tied with green string?
That's my string, off my peas. I've never given him any. Have a couple of the apples; I kept the best back. And some of the wood. Turned out fine, hasn't it.
I went up myself yesterday. He was cutting. He didn't look up. I left the string on the woodpile and came home before the dew was down.
I put the windfalls on top of the woodpile.
There's a bundle of kindling up there already, tied with green string, set square in the middle of the top log. I leave it where it is.
Split logs stacked bark up, more than one man could cut in a week. The ends on the top row are still white.
There's been a light in {place:denny_ruin} three nights running. Tramps, I expect. Nobody's lived there for years.
Would you look, by daylight, and tell me it's nothing? A courting couple, most likely. I'd take it better from somebody who's been.
{place:denny_ruin}. Inside the walls, by day. It'll be the moon on something wet. That's what I tell myself, about eleven.
Candles. And a chair.
Facing the door? Somebody wanting to see who comes in, that's all. A watchman, sort of. Take this. I won't sleep tonight either way.
Four nights now. Glow-worms, the wife says, only they don't come that colour. I go home the long way round, so I don't pass it.
Candle ends, dozens of them, burnt right down in saucers along what's left of the wall. I count to thirty and stop.
One kitchen chair, facing the doorway, nothing on it. The seat's clean. Everything else in here is under dust.
I've potatoes to lift and a back that won't have it. It's in my book: back went, Thursday, shifting the water butt.
Would you lift them for me, before the frost? The frost comes on the same night every year. I've written it down every year, and it's the same night.
In the garden, in the rows. They come up easy this year. I've put that in the book as well. Easy, I've put.
That's a good row. That's a very good row.
Bigger than I put them in. I'll weigh them and write it down. Take these from the cupboard instead; I'd like to look at those properly first.
I've looked at them. Weighed them. They're potatoes, and I've written that down. I've still put them out of the house.
What would it be, the half hour? I'd say the half hour, by the light. My clock's stopped. It stopped at nine last night.
I went out to look at the sky and dropped the key in the clearing. A little brass key. Would you find it? I don't like not knowing when it is.
In the clearing somewhere. A little brass key. You've not the time on you? No. Nor me. That's the trouble.
That's it. Thank you. Now then.
I'll set it by guess and put it right at nine, when the bell goes. Take an apple, and the water. It's about the quarter, I'd say. I'm usually near.
It's kept time since, to the minute. Except at nine every night it stops while the bell goes, and then carries on, and it's still right in the morning.
Shed door's stuck. Since Saturday. Never had a lock on it.
Shoulder to it, low down. It sticks at the bottom.
The shed. Low down.
Open?
Swept? I've not swept that shed in my life. Take that, for your shoulder.
Door stays open now. I'd sooner see in.
I put my shoulder to the door, low down. It holds, then gives all at once, and I nearly go in after it.
Inside, the floor's been swept, everywhere except a square in the middle the size of a chair. In the square, sawdust, and four dents.
A plank shed. The floor inside is swept round a square of sawdust the size of a chair, with a dent at each corner.
There's an owl in the woodpile. Aren't you, in there. I heard her Tuesday night. I won't burn a stick of it till I know the nest's empty.
Would you look? My knees won't have the bending. Now you keep still, madam. She's only looking.
The woodpile. The gap halfway up. Mind your fingers. Hear that? No. She's keeping quiet for you, aren't you, madam.
Buttons?
Owls do that. They take things. Don't you. Have some wood, from the other pile, and a flower off the step.
I'm burning the other pile first; there's plenty. Goodnight, madam, I say to it, last thing. She's not answered me yet.
A gap halfway up the woodpile, lined with straw. No owl. No feathers either, and nothing an owl leaves behind.
In the straw, three buttons: small, brown, a child's, all off the same coat. I put them back the way they were.
My brother cuts at {place:voke_brother}. We've not spoken since Easter. Easter Sunday, half past one, over the carving.
Would you take him this can of tea? Leave it by his fire. Don't say it's from me. He'll work it out.
{place:voke_brother}. By the fire. Don't say anything. He's not said a word to me since Easter, so that's fair.
Did he drink it?
No, you wouldn't know. That's fair. Have these. First apples I've picked since Easter.
There was a can on my step this morning. Empty. Washed. First thing I've had off him since Easter. I've put it on the mantel.
I leave the can on a stone by the fire, and say nothing, because I was asked not to.
A ring of stones and last night's ash. Two stones are set by it to sit on. One's worn smooth. The other has moss on it.
His tea'll be stewed if he doesn't come in. He'll be sitting out in the garden. He'll have his cup with him.
Would you tell him? Mr Grey. He'll answer to Mr Grey, I expect. It'll still be his name.
In the garden. He'll be sat with his cup. He won't have drunk it.
Not there? He'll be walking.
He'll walk a good deal, now. Take an apple, and the water. I'll keep his tea warm. I'll keep it warm till he comes.
He'll be in at ten, on the stairs. I'll hear him. His door will be locked when I go up after.
It'll have been locked since June. I'll have the only key.
A cup of tea on the path, cold, with a skin on it. Nobody in the garden.
The earth between the rows has been walked, up and back, up and back, in one very straight line. Every print is the same depth.
Would you water the seedlings? I can't carry the can any more.
From the left. You never water a seedling from the right; they sulk. My wife always did it from the left. They grow toward where she stood.
In the garden. From the left. Little and often, and never in the heat of the day. That's how it's done.
From the left? Good. That's how it's done.
They'll do now. Take these. They come up every year without me. A lily wants a north wall, you know. Everybody knows that.
They lean toward the door now. Just to the left of it. Plants know who looks after them; I've always said that. Well. She said it.
I water the row from the left, the way he asked, a little at a time.
Every seedling in the garden leans the same way: toward the house, a little to the left of the door. I look where they're looking. A worn patch on the step.
I lent the family at {place:sayer_house} my ladder in the spring, for the roof. Ladder, one, sixteen rungs, lent Lady Day. I keep a note.
I don't need it back. I'd just like to know it's still there and still mine. Would you look? I'll owe you, and I pay what I owe.
{place:sayer_house}. Off the road. It'll be against a wall. It's got my name on it, so nobody can say it was given.
Tarred? They've looked after it, then. That's a fair return.
I'll fetch it Sunday. Take these. That's you and me square.
I've not fetched it. They'll want it for the roof. I've put it in the book as still out.
A ladder, freshly tarred, stands up in the middle of the floor. It isn't leaning on anything. I don't touch it.
On the second rung, in white paint: SAYER. Under it, in a different hand: RETURN BY SUNDAY.
They had my husband's good coat off the line. The lot at {place:rendle_camp}, off the road. I know it was them.
Would you get it back? It's the coat he's to be buried in. He isn't ill. It's arranged, that's all: the coat, the plot, the two hymns. I like things arranged.
{place:rendle_camp}. They'll have it in their box. Be careful of them. I've the brush out ready for it, and the hanger.
That's it. And brushed.
Folded? It's never been folded like that; he'd crease it. Take these, with thanks. That's the coat seen to.
He wore it to church on Sunday. He said it fitted better than it used to. It's back on the hanger now, ready.
Has the bell been going early for you? It has for me. I've known since Tuesday. I'd like it proved.
Would you stand in my clearing after nine and listen, and tell me in the morning if it goes twice? There's a chalk mark where to stand.
In the clearing, after nine. On the chalk mark. Listen north, toward the hill. You'll hear it twice. I'm not often wrong about a thing like that.
Twice? I knew it. I said as much to myself on Tuesday.
I'll set my watch by the second one. Take this. You were out after nine for me and you came back, so that's proved as well.
I set my watch by the second bell now. I'm early for everything. That proves it too, if you think about it.
I stand on the chalk mark and listen north.
The bell goes at nine, from the hill. It goes again a little after, from somewhere much nearer, behind me and low down.
An X in chalk on a flat stone, where somebody wants somebody to stand. It's been chalked over more than once, each one a little north of the last.
There's a stump in the clearing the cutters have put their names in for a hundred years. Ab Morley. Jos Morley, his lad. Walt Kneebone. I can say them all.
Would you read me the newest? My eyes are going. Somebody's cut one since Friday, and nobody's been up here but me.
The old stump, in the clearing. The newest is at the bottom, under Dick Hatch. Dick went in the spring.
What did it say?
Only the year, and room for a name? Somebody's keeping a place, then. Take this, anyway. Ab, Jos, Walt, Dick. And room.
I've not cut my own name in. I'd have to go under the new one, and I'd rather not. Ab, Jos, Walt, Dick. I say them over at night instead.
Names cut in the stump, one under another, each with its year. I count back. The years go further than the tree could have stood.
The newest is at the bottom: a pale fresh cut, squared off for a name and not yet lettered, with this year beside it.
Take this to the old lady at {place:ruck_cottage}, would you? She's nobody to cut for her, so I do it, and she pays me in grapes.
She'll want to pay you. Don't let her. She's paid me in grapes every week since I was a boy, and I can't abide grapes.
{place:ruck_cottage}. Leave it at the door. Then walk off quick, before the chain comes off.
She paid you, didn't she. Grapes.
Every week since I was a boy. Have some wood as well, so you're square with somebody, which is more than I am.
She told me there was somebody new on the road. I said I'd heard. Then she gave me grapes for the news, and it was hers.
The door opens on its chain. A thin hand takes the kindling and comes back out with a paper bag of grapes.
"For your trouble. No, take it. I've always paid for my wood." The grapes are cold from the larder.
Nobody comes. Inside, somebody's laying a table, one plate at a time. I count four by the sound, and then a fifth.
